sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None of the eight lines in this section is a `no`. One finding falls outside the checklist and is given here because it touches the times a rider will act on:

1. *(No checklist line; this is a copy problem, judged by common sense.)* **The schedule numbers don't add up.** It's in the first paragraph, at about x 0–873, y 145–195. Crossings run "every forty minutes" from "seven in the morning" to "six in the evening". That's 11 hours, or 660 minutes, which isn't a whole number of 40-minute gaps. Starting at 7:00, the departures fall at 17:40 and 18:20, never at 18:00. A rider planning the last crossing can read this two ways. Either the last boat leaves at 17:40 and someone arriving at 17:50 misses it, or the gap changes at some point in the day. The times are also written as words ("seven in the morning") instead of 07:00 and 18:00, so someone scanning for a departure time has nothing to catch on. The fix: make the cadence and the end times agree, or say where they break ("every forty minutes, last crossing 17:40"). Give times as numerals, and a full list of departures if riders need one. Defect. Weight: major, because times are what riders act on and later hold the operator to.

**What's working.**
- The headline "How the river ferry runs in winter" (y ≈ 70–110) says exactly what the page covers, for whom and when. A first-time reader can sum up the page in one sentence before reading the body.
- There's no decoration. The only shape is the pale grey box (x 0–880, y 290–411), and it has a job: it separates the fare and vehicle rules from the schedule. One sans-serif and one near-black on white give a calm, practical notice. That suits a public service page.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes.

I worked from the whole image, which is 1280×800 and needed no crops, because Bash was blocked. That meant I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. Since every line came out `yes`, no entries had to be opened. Two things belong to other sections: the text sits flush against the left edge at x = 0, and the box has more padding below its text than above. I left both to those critics.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. Not a checklist line. This is my own judgment as a designer (taste), and it is minor. The tinted box at roughly x 0–880, y 290–412 gives the most emphasis on the page to bicycle and vehicle fares. The one thing the reader has to act on gets no emphasis: "Check the board at the ticket hut before you queue" at y 229–256. Someone skimming reads the boxed fare note and can miss the instruction that stops them waiting for a boat that has been held. Move the emphasis to the ice/hold instruction, or give it its own callout. The fares can stay as plain body text.

All three checklist lines answered yes. No checklist findings.

**What's working.**
- The title "How the river ferry runs in winter" (y ≈ 70–110) clearly dominates. It looks about 2.5× the body size, in bold and a darker ink, so the eye knows where to start and there is nothing competing with it.
- The scale is tight and has no near-miss sizes. I count two sizes, title and body, with a big gap between them. The callout is set apart by its tinted background, not by a third size. Every level reads at a glance.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. The page has a single column of text: a headline, two paragraphs and a tinted note.

**Findings**
1. **Do text and boxes keep a margin from the edge of the page or screen? No.** The headline, both paragraphs and the grey callout all start at x≈0, right against the left edge of the 1280 px frame. There is about 70 px of space above the headline and about 400 px to the right of the column, so the missing left margin looks like a bug, not a choice. The viewer sees a page that looks broken or half-loaded, as if a container lost its padding, and the first letters of each line ("H", "F", "W", "C") and the callout's rounded corner press against the edge. This breaks the rule that text sits inside a type area with a margin on every side (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Margin proportions" and "Construction of the type area"). Ruder also names running content up to the edge as a mark of average work. Fix: put the column inside a type area with a real left margin, at least as large as the top margin (about 70 px), and check in the live page whether a wrapper's padding or max-width centering is missing. **Defect** (the page looks broken), backed by a **convention**. Weight: **major**.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip? No.** Everything with weight, including the dark 40 px-ish headline, two text blocks and the tinted 880×120 callout, sits in the top-left block (x 0–880, y 70–412). The right 400 px and the bottom 390 px are empty, and nothing there acts as a counterweight. The page seems to slide up and left out of the frame, and the open area reads as space left over at the end rather than space that does any work. This is Arnheim's point: a heavy side needs a counterweight (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). It is likely the same root cause as finding 1. Fix: place the column on purpose, either centered in the frame with matching margins or with a deliberate left margin, so the white space reads as framing. If the empty right side is meant for something (a map, a timetable), it should hold it. **Defect** here, because it adds to the broken look. Weight: **major**, though it is largely fixed together with finding 1.
3. **Off-checklist: uneven padding inside the callout.** Inside the grey box (y≈290–412), the space above the first line of text is about 26 px, but below the last line ("the cargo deck at the stern.") it is about 46 px. The box looks like it has an empty extra line at the bottom, or a missing third line, and it adds to the unfinished feel. Fix: make the top and bottom padding equal, and check for a trailing empty element or margin inside the box. **Taste/common sense** (no catalog entry). Weight: **minor**.

**What's working.**
- The spacing groups the content correctly. The headline has about 40 px of space under it, and the paragraphs and callout sit about 20 px apart in a steady rhythm, so the piece reads as one title over one run of related notes.
- The callout text is inset by a clear 24 px inside its tint, not a near-miss. That shows it is deliberately set apart from the body text while still sharing the column's outer edges (x 0–880).

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I couldn't tell whether the flush-left column is the design or a capture or CSS glitch, such as a missing container padding or a viewport that doesn't match the layout's breakpoint. Load the page live at 1280 px and at narrower widths to check where the column sits and whether a margin appears. (Bash was refused in this session, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. I worked from the full image, which is about one screen, and read the entries directly.)

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (text and boxes keep a margin from the page edge; visual weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** No. The two paragraphs and the grey note box run as one wide column from x≈0 to x≈875 (the box text from x≈24 to x≈835), about 100 to 105 characters per line. "From November to March … The first crossing is at" is about 103. At that width the eye has to travel a long way back to the start of the next line and can land on the wrong one. That matters here because the lines hold the times a passenger needs: every forty minutes, seven in the morning, six in the evening. The paragraphs are only two lines each, which limits the damage, but the timetable facts still sit at the far right end of the first line. Bringhurst gives 45 to 75 characters for a single column, with 66 as the ideal (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.1.2, p. 26). Fix: give the text column a maximum width of about 66 characters, roughly 600 to 640 px at this size. The empty right 400 px of the canvas shows there is room to spare. Convention. Weight: minor, because the text is very short; it would become major if the page grew longer.

**What's working.**
- The text stays in one family (an Inter-like sans), with all hierarchy done through size and weight: a bold headline of about 40 px over regular body text of about 18 px. There is no second face and no in-between size, so each level has an obvious job.
- Copy is near-black on white and on the pale #EDF0F5-ish note box, so contrast is comfortably above 4.5:1 in both places. Paragraphs are separated by space only, flush left, with a gentle rag and no runts.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters)

Walk (working notes):
First read: the eye lands on the bold near-black headline at top left, then moves down through two body paragraphs to a pale blue-gray rounded box with fare information. It's an informational article or help-page excerpt about winter ferry service. It feels calm, plain and neutral. Assumed job: tell riders the winter timetable, ice delays and fares, read on a web page.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. White, near-black text and one pale cool gray tint.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. There is no saturated color.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white. The callout tint is faint but still separates in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool recede: yes. The one cool tint sits on a secondary aside.
- Matching colors look the same: yes.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. The callout is also marked by its box, padding and rounded edge.
- Dark theme background: yes. Not a dark theme.

No line came out no or unsure, so no entries need opening.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Restrained, all-neutral palette.** The page uses near-black text, a white ground and one pale cool tint on the callout at about 0–880 × 290–412 px. Nothing competes with the words, which suits a practical timetable notice.
- **The callout is set apart mostly by shape.** Its rounded box and inset padding mark it, and the faint blue-gray only supports that. The aside still reads as separate in grayscale or for viewers with color-vision deficiency, and the cool, low-saturation tint lets it sit back as secondary information.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks. It holds only a headline, two body paragraphs and a shaded note box.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The right side of the page is empty, from about x 880 to 1280, and so is everything below the note box, from about y 412 down. This could be an image slot that never loaded, since screenshots often catch a page before its pictures appear. Nothing on the page shows a broken image or a placeholder, so this is not a finding. Load the page in a browser and check whether a picture should be there.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
